e.t: Abiud is a personal name, referring to a man named Abiud in the Greek New Testament. The name appears twice in the underlying text, both within one verse reference: Matthew 1:13. Because no broader definition or descriptive meaning is provided, Abiud should be understood primarily as the person’s name rather than as a word expressing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. Its precise significance in Matthew 1:13 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Impartial means treating people or matters without favoring one side over another. It describes even-handed conduct that is not driven by personal preference, advantage, or bias. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in James 3:17. Its precise force there comes from the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains clear: refusing to tilt toward a preferred person or position. It therefore points to fairness and freedom from favoritism rather than biased judgment.

This word refers to a captive or prisoner—someone held under another power and unable to act freely. It describes people in a condition of confinement or subjection, rather than expressing an action or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 4:18. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person who has been taken captive or kept as a prisoner.

This Greek New Testament word means “salt spring” or “salty,” describing something marked by saltiness or associated with a salt spring. Its central idea is a salty quality rather than sweetness or freshness. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in James 3:12, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

This word means “lawlessness” or “wickedness”—conduct that disregards what is right and refuses rightful boundaries. It names wrongdoing as a condition or pattern, not merely an isolated mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it can describe people whose outward appearance hides inward evil, the increase of wrongdoing, or the sinful state from which forgiveness is needed. The word occurs 15 times in 13 verses, showing that it is used across several New Testament settings to describe serious opposition to righteousness.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to die,” describing the ending of life or the act of dying. Its related forms can express that someone “died,” “dies,” “will die,” or has already died. The word appears 111 times across the Greek New Testament, showing that death is discussed in many kinds of passages. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on who is said to die and how the surrounding sentence presents the event.

e.t: This word means “to fall away” or “to fall from.” It describes movement in which someone or something comes down and separates from a place, position, or attachment. The wording can emphasize either the departure itself or the point from which the person or thing falls. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 9:18. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its central idea is falling away or falling from something.

This word means “confirmation”—something that makes a matter firm, settled, or assured. It points to established certainty rather than a mere possibility or unsupported claim. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “confirmation.” The word appears in Philippians 1:7 and Hebrews 6:16, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific role in each passage. Its central idea remains the strengthening or settling of what is affirmed.

This word means “prize”—an award or reward set before someone who is striving toward a goal. It refers to something pursued and received at the end of determined effort, rather than merely describing the effort itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians and Philippians, and both occurrences use the same rendering. Its precise significance in either verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a prize held out to the one pressing toward the goal.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb describes begetting a child, becoming a father, or being born. It can therefore refer either to the parent’s action in bringing forth a child or to the child’s birth, depending on how it functions in the sentence. The word occurs 97 times in the Greek New Testament, across 65 verses, so it is used broadly in genealogical records and in statements about birth and spiritual life. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: This word means “to discuss” or “to talk about” something. It describes people speaking together about a matter, rather than merely making an isolated sound or statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke, and its basic sense remains conversation or discussion. The surrounding passage determines exactly what the people were discussing and what attitude accompanied their words, but the word itself points to verbal exchange about a subject.

This word means “difficult” or “hard,” describing something that is not easy to do, accept, or accomplish. It functions as an adjective, marking the demanding nature of whatever it describes rather than naming a person or thing by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: a serious obstacle or demanding situation.

This word refers to a descendant, especially a grandchild. It identifies a person who comes from a family line, with “grandchild” being a more specific sense of the broader meaning “descendant.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 5:4. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to family descent and a younger generation within the household or family line.

This word means an inscription: writing placed on or attached to something, such as a displayed notice or identifying text. It is a noun that refers to the written wording itself rather than to the object bearing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, and its normal sense remains focused on an inscription or written title. The precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to explain.” It describes making something understandable by opening up its meaning or significance to another person. The word functions as an action, focusing on the act of clarifying rather than merely mentioning or repeating something. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 4:34 and Acts 19:39, showing that its basic sense is a clear, deliberate explanation whose precise force depends on the surrounding passage.

Hezron is a personal name referring to a person in the genealogical records of the New Testament. It does not function as a description or action word; it identifies an individual by name. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in two verses: twice in Matthew 1:3 and once in Luke 3:33. Because the available passages identify the person by name without providing a separate definition, its ordinary meaning here is simply the proper name Hezron.

Eunice is a personal name, identifying a woman rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Timothy 1:5. The available rendering preserves it as “Eunice,” showing that it functions as a person’s name rather than as a translated common noun. Its specific significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the information stated there about the person who bears the name.

e.h: A Yoke or Set of Scales
e.t: This word means a yoke, the bar or harness joining animals for work, and it can also refer to scales used for weighing. As a yoke, it can describe a literal implement or, by comparison, a burden, obligation, or form of service placed upon people. The Greek New Testament uses it six times, including language about taking a yoke, bearing one, or being under one. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Joanna is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs twice, and both occurrences are in Luke. Its meaning is therefore simply the name Joanna; the surrounding passage identifies the person being mentioned in each occurrence. The name appears in Luke 8:3 and Luke 24:10.

This word means “straw” or “stubble,” referring to the dry stalks left after grain has been harvested. It describes a light, easily burned material rather than something durable or valuable like stone or precious metal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 3:12. Its basic meaning is therefore a common, fragile building material, though the surrounding verse is needed to explain how the image is being used there.

This word means “centurion,” referring to a person identified by that title. It is used three times in the Greek New Testament, and all three occurrences appear in Mark 15. Because the word itself identifies a particular role or title rather than describing an action, its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage. The term appears in Mark 15:39, 15:44, and 15:45, where the same word is consistently rendered “centurion.”

This word means “power”—the ability or force to accomplish something, prevail, or exercise authority. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for power associated with God, his works, and those who act with strength or authority. Its repeated rendering as “power” supports this central sense. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of God’s power and the power believers are urged to draw upon.

This word means “blessed,” describing a person who is in a favorable or honored condition. It is used of people whom Jesus declares blessed, including those who are poor in spirit, hunger for righteousness, or make peace. It can also describe those who see what God’s servants longed to see, or those who believe God’s promise. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 50 times, from Matthew through Revelation, functioning as a statement of blessing or favorable standing.

Melea is a personal name. It does not describe an action, quality, object, or relationship; it identifies an individual by name. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Luke 3:31, and the English rendering preserves it as “Melea.” Its meaning is chiefly its role as a personal designation, not a concept to translate into an ordinary descriptive word.

This word means “mediator”—a person who stands between two parties to help establish or maintain a relationship between them. It identifies someone who serves as an intermediary rather than acting as one of the parties themselves. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Galatians, 1 Timothy, and Hebrews. Its precise role in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding context.

Nathanael is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears six times, all in John’s Gospel. It is used consistently as “Nathanael,” including references in John 1 and John 21. The name itself identifies the person; the surrounding passage is needed to understand what Nathanael says or does in any particular verse.

Victory means triumph or success over an opposing power, difficulty, or challenge. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, in 1 John 5:4, and its English rendering there is “victory.” It names the outcome of overcoming rather than the struggle itself. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how John applies that idea in context, but the word’s central sense remains a gained victory or triumph.

This word means confession: an open acknowledgment or declaration of what one believes or affirms. It functions as a noun, naming the confession itself rather than the act of confessing as a verb. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, consistently rendered “confession.” Its occurrences are found in 2 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, and Hebrews, so the word serves a recurring role in New Testament language.

This word means “old”. It describes something that has existed for a long time or belongs to an earlier period, serving as a simple description of age or former use. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times, including passages that speak of old garments, old wineskins, and old things. Its basic sense remains consistent: it identifies something as not new. The surrounding verse determines what particular object, practice, or thing is being called old.

e.t: This word means “to surround”—to be positioned around someone or something. It describes an encircling presence rather than merely being nearby. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including uses in Mark, Luke, Acts, and Hebrews. The surrounding thing may be understood from the sentence and its wider context, but the word itself centers on being encompassed or enclosed on all sides. Its basic sense remains consistent wherever it appears.

This word means “manifold,” describing something that has many forms, aspects, or expressions rather than only one. It points to richness and variety within a single whole. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 3:10, so its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains clear: something manifold is diverse, varied, and made up of many distinct features or dimensions.

This Greek New Testament word means “fish,” referring to the aquatic animal. It is a concrete word that names something rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 21:5. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text, but its basic lexical sense remains simple: a fish. The word’s identity and gloss establish this ordinary meaning, while the single occurrence indicates that it is uncommon in this corpus.

This word means “early” or “morning,” referring to the beginning part of the day. It describes the time associated with dawn or the morning rather than a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are in Revelation. Its basic sense remains a simple time reference; the surrounding verse determines the precise force of that reference. The word appears in Revelation 2:28 and Revelation 22:16.

e.t: This word means “clearly” or “expressly,” describing something stated in a plain, direct, and unmistakable way. It points to a message that is openly declared rather than hinted at or left uncertain. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 4:1, so its normal meaning is especially concise: what is communicated expressly is made clear for others to recognize. The surrounding verse supplies the specific message being declared.

This word means “linen,” referring to cloth made from flax. It is a noun describing a material used as fabric or wrapping cloth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages describing linen associated with clothing and burial. Its repeated rendering as “linen” supports this straightforward meaning, while the surrounding verse determines the particular use of the cloth. References include Matthew 27:59, Mark 14:51–52 and 15:46, and Luke 23:53.

This word means “worm,” referring to the creature itself. It is a concrete noun rather than a description of an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 9:48, and both recorded English renderings use “worm.” Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic meaning remains direct and consistent: a worm.

e.t: This word means “to reign with,” describing shared rule or royal authority together with another. It expresses participation in reigning rather than ruling alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians 4:8 and 2 Timothy 2:12. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: to share in the exercise or enjoyment of kingship. The surrounding verse determines who reigns together and how that shared reign relates to the passage’s wider message.

This Greek New Testament word refers to an “offering for slaughter” or a “sacrificial victim”—something designated to be offered in sacrifice. It names the victim or offering itself rather than describing a broader spiritual idea or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 7:42, so repeated passages do not provide a wider range of usage. Its central meaning remains a victim presented for sacrifice.

This word means “therefore,” drawing a conclusion from what has just been said. It links an earlier statement, fact, or instruction with the response or conclusion that follows. In ordinary reading, it signals that the next words should be understood as resulting from, or being supported by, the preceding message. This Greek New Testament word occurs twice in the corpus, in 1 Thessalonians 4:8 and Hebrews 12:1. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central function remains a clear connecting word: because of what came before, this follows.

This word means “footstool,” a low support on which someone rests the feet. It names an ordinary object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, showing a consistent meaning across its uses. Several passages use the word in language about placing something beneath the feet, but the precise force of each passage depends on its surrounding verse and context.

Philetus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Timothy 2:17. The available wording preserves the name as “Philetus,” so its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader who a person is called. The surrounding passage is needed to understand this person’s particular role or significance there; the name itself does not provide that information.
